## The finish line

By the end of this course you can take a deviation from discovery all the way through a CAPA
effectiveness check. You can also explain document control and change control well enough to
defend them to an AABB assessor or an FDA investigator.

This is the machinery underneath everything a blood center's Quality function does. You
already run most of it under ITIL names: incident, problem, change, knowledge. This course
gives you the names, records, and expectations an assessor uses, and shows where the quality
version asks for more than the IT version you know.

## Before you start

This course assumes all three foundations and the first course:

- [Reading a CFR citation](../../foundations/reading-a-cfr-citation/index.qmd)
- [Regulatory landscape orientation](../../foundations/regulatory-landscape-orientation/index.qmd)
  — regulation vs. guidance vs. AABB Standard vs. industry practice matters in every module here.
- [Risk and controls vocabulary](../../foundations/risk-and-controls-vocabulary/index.qmd)
  — likelihood, severity, detectability, and preventive/detective/corrective controls are
  used here as words you already own. Module 6 builds on them; it doesn't re-teach them.
- [Blood Center Operations](../blood-center-operations/index.qmd) — especially
  [BECS in the pipeline](../blood-center-operations/becs-in-the-pipeline/index.qmd), which
  set up the "one incident, two tracks" idea and the tension between change control and
  validation that this course picks up.

## The seven modules

Each module is one sitting, and each has its own finish line.

1. **The AABB quality system at a glance** — name the parts of AABB's Quality System
   Essentials (QSEs), place any quality activity in the right one, and say how the framework
   mirrors ISO 9001 and the ITIL practices you already run.
2. **Deviations and nonconformances** — take an unplanned event from discovery through
   containment, impact assessment, product disposition, and a documented reportability
   decision, and say when it needs a CAPA.
3. **CAPA: root cause to effectiveness check** — tell a real root cause from "human error,"
   pick corrective and preventive actions that change the process, and set an effectiveness
   check that could actually fail.
4. **Change control for regulated systems** — take any change to a regulated process,
   document, piece of equipment, or system through request, impact assessment, approval,
   implementation, and verification, and name the record behind each step.
5. **Document control and records** — follow a controlled document from draft to retirement,
   tell a document from a record, and explain how an obsolete version ends up in use and what
   stops it.
6. **Quality risk management** — run a quality decision through ICH Q9's risk management
   process with an FMEA or risk ranking and filtering, and decide how much formality the
   decision deserves.
7. **Internal audits and management review** — explain what internal assessments do inside
   the quality system and what management review has to do with their results, and judge
   whether a management-review packet shows a quality system that works.

Modules 2 through 5 follow one event at Lakeshore Blood Center from the day it's found to the
day the fix is proven. Module 6 steps back and formalizes the risk calls those modules made.
Module 7 closes the loop: how the organization finds out whether all of it is working. It
also hands off to `fda-and-aabb-in-practice`, the next course in this track, which covers
designing a full audit program and facing inspectors.

Modules appear in the sidebar as they're built.
